entries.6af28abae6d7e6707a6ed852ac7bab900ad37121: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13893"/><div sID="gen26739" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13893"/><hi type="bold">7. And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up, and choked it, and it yielded no fruit--</hi>This case is that of ground not thoroughly cleaned of the thistles, &c.; which, rising above the good seed, "choke" or "smother" it, excluding light and air, and drawing away the moisture and richness of the soil. Hence it "becomes unfruitful" (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.22">Mt 13:22</reference>); it grows, but its growth is checked, and it never ripens. The evil here is neither a hard nor a shallow soil--there is softness enough, and depth enough; but it is the existence in it of what draws all the moisture and richness of the soil away to itself, and so starves the plant. What now are these "thorns?" See on <reference osisRef="Mark.4.19">Mr 4:19</reference>.<div eID="gen26739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26740" type="x-p"/> Fourth Case: The Good Ground. (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.8">Mr 4:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.4.20">20</reference>). <div eID="gen26740" type="x-p"/>
entries.59805ab9aafc02727637534f1dd71071531bc2de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13894"/><div sID="gen26741" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13894"/><hi type="bold">8. And other fell on good ground, and did yield fruit, &c.--</hi>The goodness of this last soil consists in its qualities being precisely the reverse of the other three soils: from its softness and tenderness, receiving and cherishing the seed; from its depth, allowing it to take firm root, and not quickly losing its moisture; and from its cleanness, giving its whole vigor and sap to the plant. In such a soil the seed "brings forth fruit," in all different degrees of profusion, according to the measure in which the soil possesses those qualities. See on <reference osisRef="Mark.4.20">Mr 4:20</reference>. <div eID="gen26741" type="x-p"/>
entries.6963f029cd48ad9e1339ff6dd3ee85630260e008: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13895"/><div sID="gen26742" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13895"/>9. And he said unto them, He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.<div eID="gen26742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26743" type="x-p"/> After this parable is recorded the Evangelist says: <div eID="gen26743" type="x-p"/>
entries.503d4609d97b7259dd77cfdfb9018dd5625bbc84: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13896"/><div sID="gen26744" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13896"/><hi type="bold">10. And when he was alone, they that were about him with the twelve--</hi>probably those who followed Him most closely and were firmest in discipleship, next to the Twelve.<div eID="gen26744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">asked of him the parable--</hi>The reply would seem to intimate that this parable of the sower was of that fundamental, comprehensive, and introductory character which we have assigned to it (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.1">Mt 13:1</reference>).<div eID="gen26745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26746" type="x-p"/> Reason for Teaching in Parables (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.11">Mr 4:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.21-Mark.12.25">12, 21-25</reference>). <div eID="gen26746" type="x-p"/>
entries.2587113dca6016dd701d51bf44c2921ee5a1c0c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13897"/><div sID="gen26747" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13897"/><hi type="bold">11-12. And he said unto them, Unto you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God: but unto them, &c.--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.10-Matt.13.17">Mt 13:10-17</reference>. <div eID="gen26747" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d7e31e9644c457e1db93aa304aeb2a0a2eff221: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13898"/><div sID="gen26748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13898"/><hi type="bold">13. Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?--</hi>Probably this was said not so much in the spirit of rebuke, as to call their attention to the exposition of it which He was about to give, and so train them to the right apprehension of His future parables. As in the parables which we have endeavored to explain in Mt 13., we shall take this parable and the Lord's own exposition of the different parts of it together. <div eID="gen26748" type="x-p"/>
entries.f230ee1984d7199914c4ac10d4bc472e7c88b50b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13899"/><div sID="gen26749" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13899"/><hi type="bold">14. The sower soweth the word--</hi>or, as in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.11">Lu 8:11</reference>), "Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God." But who is "the sower?" This is not expressed here because if "the word of God" be the seed, every scatterer of that precious seed must be regarded as a sower. It is true that in the parable of the tares it is said, "He that soweth the good seed is the Son of man," as "He that soweth the tares is the devil" (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.37">Mt 13:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.38">38</reference>). But these are only the great unseen parties, struggling in this world for the possession of man. Each of these has his agents among men themselves; and Christ's agents in the sowing of the good seed are the preachers of the word. Thus, as in all the cases about to be described, the sower is the same, and the seed is the same; while the result is entirely different, the whole difference must lie in the soils, which mean the different states of the human heart. And so, the great general lesson held forth in this parable of the sower is, that however faithful the preacher, and how pure soever his message, the effect of the preaching of the word depends upon the state of the hearer's heart. Now follow the cases. See on <reference osisRef="Mark.4.4">Mr 4:4</reference>. <div eID="gen26749" type="x-p"/>
entries.b9a7dfc2c85bb4bf29d6d163eac79b07a449473e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13900"/><div sID="gen26750" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13900"/><hi type="bold">15. And these are they by the wayside, where the word is sown; but, when they have heard, &c.--</hi>or, more fully (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.19">Mt 13:19</reference>), "When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart." The great truth here taught is, that hearts all unbroken and hard are no fit soil for saving truth. They apprehend it not (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.19">Mt 13:19</reference>) as God's means of restoring them to Himself; it penetrates not, makes no impression, but lies loosely on the surface of the heart, till the wicked one--afraid of losing a victim by his "believing to salvation" (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.12">Lu 8:12</reference>)--finds some frivolous subject by whose greater attractions to draw off the attention, and straightway it is gone. Of how many hearers of the word is this the graphic but painful history! <div eID="gen26750" type="x-p"/>
entries.b18569245e96699e6c00938a21c47e549eff6512: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13901"/><div sID="gen26751" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13901"/><hi type="bold">16. And these are they likewise which are sown on stony ground, &c.--</hi>"Immediately" the seed in such a case "springs up"--all the quicker from the shallowness of the soil--"because it has no depth of earth." But the sun, beating on it, as quickly scorches and withers it up, "because it has no root" (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.6">Mr 4:6</reference>), and "lacks moisture" (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.6">Lu 8:6</reference>). The great truth here taught is that hearts superficially impressed are apt to receive the truth with readiness, and even with joy (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.13">Lu 8:13</reference>); but the heat of tribulation or persecution because of the word, or the trials which their new profession brings upon them quickly dries up their relish for the truth, and withers all the hasty promise of fruit which they showed. Such disappointing issues of a faithful and awakening ministry--alas, how frequent are they! <div eID="gen26751" type="x-p"/>
entries.e8aa60e1ef0cb3b90e6b220fd01950b9ac1f9d8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13902"/><div sID="gen26752" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13902"/>18. And these are they which are sown among thorns; such as hear the word, <div eID="gen26752" type="x-p"/>
entries.48b87ff80b1431ad0144e9be40d1c30d02cd22ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13903"/><div sID="gen26753" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13903"/><hi type="bold">19. And the cares of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things entering in--</hi>or "the pleasures of this life" (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.14">Lu 8:14</reference>).<div eID="gen26753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26754" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">choke the word, and it becometh unfruitful--</hi>First, "The cares of this world"--anxious, unrelaxing attention to the business of this present life; second, "The deceitfulness of riches"--of those riches which are the fruit of this worldly "care"; third, "The pleasures of this life," or "the lusts of other things entering in"--the enjoyments in themselves may be innocent, which worldly prosperity enables one to indulge. These "choke" or "smother" the word; drawing off so much of one's attention, absorbing so much of one's interest, and using up so much of one's time, that only the dregs of these remain for spiritual things, and a fagged, hurried, and heartless formalism is at length all the religion of such persons. What a vivid picture is this of the mournful condition of many, especially in great commercial countries, who once promised much fruit! "They bring no fruit to perfection" (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.14">Lu 8:14</reference>); indicating how much growth there may be, in the early stages of such a case, and promise of fruit--which after all never ripens. <div eID="gen26754" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6c8515731d67fadab080e2df1b3058271bd3d04: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13904"/><div sID="gen26755" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13904"/><hi type="bold">20. And these are they which are sown on good ground; such as hear the word, and receive it, and bring forth fruit, some thirtyfold, some sixty, and some an hundred--</hi>A heart soft and tender, stirred to its depths on the great things of eternity, and jealously guarded from worldly engrossments, such only is the "honest and good heart" (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.15">Lu 8:15</reference>), which "keeps," that is, "retains" the seed of the word, and bears fruit just in proportion as it is such a heart. Such "bring forth fruit with patience" (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.15">Mr 4:15</reference>), or continuance, "enduring to the end"; in contrast with those in whom the word is "choked" and brings no fruit to perfection. The "thirtyfold" is designed to express the lowest degree of fruitfulness; the "hundredfold" the highest; and the "sixtyfold" the intermediate degrees of fruitfulness. As a "hundredfold," though not unexampled (<reference osisRef="Gen.26.12">Ge 26:12</reference>), is a rare return in the natural husbandry, so the highest degrees of spiritual fruitfulness are too seldom witnessed. The closing words of this introductory parable seem designed to call attention to the fundamental and universal character of it. <div eID="gen26755" type="x-p"/>
entries.154a5d18e7a8d5004c5e571cb50ae9eb12d95109: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13905"/><div sID="gen26756" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13905"/><hi type="bold">21. And he said unto them, Is a candle--</hi>or "lamp"<div eID="gen26756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brought to be put under a bushel, or under a bed? and not to be set on a candlestick?--</hi>"that they which enter in may see the light" (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.16">Lu 8:16</reference>). See on <reference osisRef="Matt.5.15">Mt 5:15</reference>, of which this is nearly a repetition. <div eID="gen26757" type="x-p"/>
entries.9deb627218efeb2c8ddb531e4e14082843224c6a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13906"/><div sID="gen26758" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13906"/><hi type="bold">22. For there is nothing hid which shall not be manifested, &c.--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Matt.10.26">Mt 10:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.27">27</reference>; but the connection there and here is slightly different. Here the idea seems to be this--"I have privately expounded to you these great truths, but only that ye may proclaim them publicly; and if ye will not, others will. For these are not designed for secrecy. They are imparted to be diffused abroad, and they shall be so; yea, a time is coming when the most hidden things shall be brought to light." <div eID="gen26758" type="x-p"/>
entries.6c64c9a534905730bf72983d21e7d08a84420834: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13907"/><div sID="gen26759" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13907"/><hi type="bold">23. If any man have ears to hear, let him hear--</hi>This for the second time on the same subject (see on <reference osisRef="Mark.4.9">Mr 4:9</reference>). <div eID="gen26759" type="x-p"/>
entries.488ed74b4fc3a3666f65b9da54e2b159f82d48a5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13908"/><div sID="gen26760" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13908"/><hi type="bold">24. And he saith unto them, Take heed what ye hear--</hi>In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.18">Lu 8:18</reference>) it is, "Take heed how ye hear." The one implies the other, but both precepts are very weighty.<div eID="gen26760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26761" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Matt.7.2">Mt 7:2</reference>.<div eID="gen26761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26762" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and unto you that hear--</hi>that is, thankfully, teachably, profitably.<div eID="gen26762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26763" type="x-p"/> shall more be given. <div eID="gen26763" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1a85dfd805b812d430775f117fdbc1a56ccd67a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13909"/><div sID="gen26764" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13909"/><hi type="bold">25. For he that hath, to him shall be given; and he that hath not, from him shall be taken even that which he hath--</hi>or "seemeth to have," or "thinketh he hath." (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.12">Mt 13:12</reference>). This "having" and "thinking he hath" are not different; for when it hangs loosely upon him, and is not appropriated to its proper ends and uses, it both is and is not his.<div eID="gen26764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26765" type="x-p"/> Parable of the Seed Growing We Know Not How (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.26-Mark.4.29">Mr 4:26-29</reference>).<div eID="gen26765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26766" type="x-p"/> This beautiful parable is peculiar to Mark. Its design is to teach the Imperceptible Growth of the word sown in the heart, from its earliest stage of development to the ripest fruits of practical righteousness. <div eID="gen26766" type="x-p"/>
entries.50c7b811f87c9e49c03a77bcd7d46d04f00a0839: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13910"/><div sID="gen26767" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13910"/><hi type="bold">26-27. So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the ground; and should sleep, and rise night and day--</hi>go about his other ordinary occupations, leaving it to the well-known laws of vegetation under the genial influences of heaven. This is the sense of "the earth bringing forth fruit of herself," in <reference osisRef="Mark.4.27">Mr 4:27</reference>. <div eID="gen26767" type="x-p"/>
entries.76bbe256b9487675d116b6cb59c205229e083b12: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13911"/><div sID="gen26768" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13911"/><hi type="bold">28. For the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself; first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear--</hi>beautiful allusion to the succession of similar stages, though not definitely marked periods, in the Christian life, and generally in the kingdom of God. <div eID="gen26768" type="x-p"/>
entries.046e69c3a351e8b28f05c2f80ba7d645133f4f3f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13912"/><div sID="gen26769" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13912"/><hi type="bold">29. But when the fruit is brought forth--</hi>to maturity<div eID="gen26769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26770" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">immediately he putteth in the sickle, because the harvest is come--</hi>This charmingly points to the transition from the earthly to the heavenly condition of the Christian and the Church.<div eID="gen26770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26771" type="x-p"/> Parable of the Mustard Seed (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.30-Mark.4.32">Mr 4:30-32</reference>).<div eID="gen26771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26772" type="x-p"/> For the exposition of this portion, see on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.31">Mt 13:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.32">32</reference>. <div eID="gen26772" type="x-p"/>
entries.70901b000c4c5f1688a5012c7c25816d4399e972: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13913"/><div sID="gen26773" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13913"/><hi type="bold">33. And with many such parables spake he the word unto them, as they were able to hear it--</hi>Had this been said in the corresponding passage of Matthew, we should have concluded that what that Evangelist recorded was but a specimen of other parables spoken on the same occasion. But Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.34">Mt 13:34</reference>) says, "All these things spake Jesus unto the multitude in parables"; and as Mark records only some of the parables which Matthew gives, we are warranted to infer that the "many such parables" alluded to here mean no more than the full complement of them which we find in Matthew. <div eID="gen26773" type="x-p"/>
entries.f601ab4a936d3ab7aee2ae4caa91e607b13d23fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13914"/><div sID="gen26774" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13914"/><hi type="bold">34. But without a parable spake he not unto them--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.34">Mt 13:34</reference>.<div eID="gen26774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26775" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and when they were alone, he expounded all things to his disciples--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Mark.4.22">Mr 4:22</reference>.<div eID="gen26775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Mark.4.35-Mark.5.20">Mr 4:35-5:20</reference>. Jesus Crossing the Sea of Galilee, Miraculously Stills a Tempest--</hi>He Cures the Demoniac of Gadara. ( = <reference osisRef="Matt.8.23-Matt.8.34">Mt 8:23-34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.8.22-Luke.8.39">Lu 8:22-39</reference>).<div eID="gen26776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26777" type="x-p"/> The time of this section is very definitely marked by our Evangelist, and by him alone, in the opening words.<div eID="gen26777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26778" type="x-p"/> Jesus Stills a Tempest on the Sea of Galilee (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.35-Mark.4.41">Mr 4:35-41</reference>). <div eID="gen26778" type="x-p"/>
entries.54df0cae8a2aa594df80602d446413d651063ccd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13915"/><div sID="gen26779" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13915"/><hi type="bold">35. And the same day--</hi>on which He spoke the memorable parables of the <reference osisRef="Mark.4.1-Mark.4.32">Mr 4:1-32</reference>, and of <reference osisRef="Matt.13.1-Matt.13.52">Mt 13:1-52</reference>.<div eID="gen26779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26780" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when the even was come--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.35">Mr 6:35</reference>). This must have been the earlier evening--what we should call the afternoon--since after all that passed on the other side, when He returned to the west side, the people were waiting for Him in great numbers (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.21">Mr 4:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.8.40">Lu 8:40</reference>).<div eID="gen26780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26781" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he saith unto them, Let us pass over unto the other side--</hi>to the east side of the lake, to grapple with a desperate case of possession, and set the captive free, and to give the Gadarenes an opportunity of hearing the message of salvation, amid the wonder which that marvellous cure was fitted to awaken and the awe which the subsequent events could not but strike into them. <div eID="gen26781" type="x-p"/>
entries.c7f2d1153e58e71c5c073e8707351f502fdedbc3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13916"/><div sID="gen26782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13916"/><hi type="bold">36. And when they had sent away the multitude, they took him even as he was in the ship--</hi>that is, without any preparation, and without so much as leaving the vessel, out of which He had been all day teaching.<div eID="gen26782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26783" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And there were also with him other little ships--</hi>with passengers, probably, wishing to accompany Him. <div eID="gen26783" type="x-p"/>
entries.bbf33fdee48f26f52efc6620aef35e7e412f057d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13917"/><div sID="gen26784" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13917"/><hi type="bold">37. And there arose a great storm of wind--</hi>"a tempest of wind." To such sudden squalls the Sea of Galilee is very liable from its position, in a deep basin, skirted on the east by lofty mountain ranges, while on the west the hills are intersected by narrow gorges through which the wind sweeps across the lake, and raises its waters with great rapidity into a storm.<div eID="gen26784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26785" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the waves beat into the ship--</hi>kept beating or pitching on the ship.<div eID="gen26785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so that it was now full--</hi>rather, "so that it was already filling." In Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.24">Mt 8:24</reference>), "insomuch that the ship was covered with the waves"; but this is too strong. It should be, "so that the ship was getting covered by the waves." So we must translate the word used in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.23">Lu 8:23</reference>)--not as in our version--"And there came down a storm on the lake, and they were filled [with water]"--but "they were getting filled," that is, those who sailed; meaning, of course, that their ship was so. <div eID="gen26786" type="x-p"/>
entries.c92fde5371e32249e670deb36e2b6d0da731463b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13918"/><div sID="gen26787" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13918"/><hi type="bold">38. And he was in the hinder part of the ship--</hi>or stern.<div eID="gen26787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26788" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">asleep on a pillow--</hi>either a place in the vessel made to receive the head, or a cushion for the head to rest on. It was evening; and after the fatigues of a busy day of teaching under the hot sun, having nothing to do while crossing the lake, He sinks into a deep sleep, which even this tempest raging around and tossing the little vessel did not disturb.<div eID="gen26788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26789" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and they awake him, and say unto him, Master--</hi>or "Teacher." In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.24">Lu 8:24</reference>) this is doubled--in token of their life-and-death earnestness--"Master, Master."<div eID="gen26789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26790" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">carest thou not that we perish?--</hi>Unbelief and fear made them sadly forget their place, to speak so. Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.25">Mt 8:25</reference>) has it, "Lord, save us, we perish." When those accustomed to fish upon that deep thus spake, the danger must have been imminent. They say nothing of what would become of Him, if they perished; nor think, whether, if He could not perish, it was likely He would let this happen to them; but they hardly knew what they said. <div eID="gen26790" type="x-p"/>
entries.c53774f6ee9e31f5149236a4e79e7b5da2da7678: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13919"/><div sID="gen26791" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13919"/><hi type="bold">39. And he arose, and rebuked the wind--</hi>"and the raging of the water" (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.24">Lu 8:24</reference>).<div eID="gen26791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26792" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and said unto the sea, Peace, be still--</hi>two sublime words of command, from a Master to His servants, the elements.<div eID="gen26792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26793" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm--</hi>The sudden hushing of the wind would not at once have calmed the sea, whose commotion would have settled only after a considerable time. But the word of command was given to both elements at once. <div eID="gen26793" type="x-p"/>
entries.ccc74ad455b9cdd64c08ba09bb73dcf74d780b3d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13920"/><div sID="gen26794" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13920"/><hi type="bold">40. And he said unto them, Why are ye so fearful?--</hi>There is a natural apprehension under danger; but there was unbelief in their fear. It is worthy of notice how considerately the Lord defers this rebuke till He had first removed the danger, in the midst of which they would not have been in a state to listen to anything.<div eID="gen26794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how is it that ye have no faith?--</hi>next to none, or none in present exercise. In Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.26">Mt 8:26</reference>) it is, "Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith?" Faith they had, for they applied to Christ for relief: but little, for they were afraid, though Christ was in the ship. Faith dispels fear, but only in proportion to its strength. <div eID="gen26795" type="x-p"/>
entries.2291845ec8af6a0a70fba7491db7c4010fea3a66: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13921"/><div sID="gen26796" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13921"/><hi type="bold">41. And they feared exceedingly--</hi>were struck with deep awe.<div eID="gen26796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26797" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and said one to another, What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?--</hi>"What is this? Israel has all along been singing of Jehovah, 'Thou rulest the raging of the sea: when the waves thereof arise, Thou stillest them!' 'The Lord on high is mightier than the noise of many waters, yea, than the mighty waves of the sea!' (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.9">Psa 89:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.93.4">93:4</reference>). But, lo, in this very boat of ours is One of our own flesh and blood, who with His word of command hath done the same! Exhausted with the fatigues of the day, He was but a moment ago in a deep sleep, undisturbed by the howling tempest, and we had to waken Him with the cry of our terror; but rising at our call, His majesty was felt by the raging elements, for they were instantly hushed--'What Manner of Man is this?'" <chapter eID="Mark.4"/>

entries.68173d39f0b69e65f991f3d07c09018d921d5bf0: <div eID="gen39208" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen39209" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39210" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39210" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39209" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39211" type="x-p"/> The parable of the sower, <reference osisRef="Mar.4.1-Mar.4.9">Mar 4:1-9</reference>. Its interpretation, <reference osisRef="Mar.4.10-Mar.4.20">Mar 4:10-20</reference>. The use we should make of the instructions we receive, <reference osisRef="Mar.4.21-Mar.4.26">Mar 4:21-26</reference>. The parable of the progressively growing seed, <reference osisRef="Mar.4.26-Mar.4.29">Mar 4:26-29</reference>. Of the mustard seed, <reference osisRef="Mar.4.30-Mar.4.34">Mar 4:30-34</reference>. Christ and his disciples are overtaken by a storm, <reference osisRef="Mar.4.35-Mar.4.38">Mar 4:35-38</reference>. He rebukes the wind and the sea, and produces fair weather, <reference osisRef="Mar.4.39-Mar.4.41">Mar 4:39-41</reference>.
entries.a399aa1616dece111d6c4d924c634b399ea06dbd: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen39211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39212" type="x-p"/> He taught them many things by parables - See every part of this parable of the sower explained on <reference osisRef="Mat.13.1">Mat 13:1</reference> (note), etc.
entries.100caff252154273f83ca86c4cdb6ec05dc9aee8: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen39212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39213" type="x-p"/> The fowls - Του ουρανου, of the air, is the common reading; but it should be omitted, on the authority of nine uncial MSS., upwards of one hundred others, and almost all the versions. Bengel and Griesbach have left it out of the text. It seems to have been inserted in Mark, from <reference osisRef="Luk.8.5">Luk 8:5</reference>.
entries.2ee25e992d7b1dfa6f6e848a852e290729dd025c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen39213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39214" type="x-p"/> And he said - He that hath ears to hear, let him hear - The Codex Bezae, later Syriac in the margin, and seven copies of the Itala, add, και ὁ συνιων συνιετω, and whoso understandeth, let him understand.
entries.0405786dd76f04db9c1128306468a7102204a17c: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen39214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39215" type="x-p"/> They that were about him - None of the other evangelists intimate that there were any besides the twelve with him: but it appears there were several others present; and though they were not styled disciples, yet they appear to have seriously attended to his public and private instructions.
entries.9d06b900eb53b9f0fee86e47bdbb9a664596ae17: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen39215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39216" type="x-p"/> Unto you it is given to know - Γνωναι, to know, is omitted by ABKL, ten others, the Coptic, and one of the Itala. The omission of this word makes a material alteration in the sense; for without it the passage may be read thus: - To you the mystery of the kingdom of God is given; but all these things are transacted in parables to those without. Griesbach leaves it doubtful. And Professor White says, probabiliter delendum. I should be inclined to omit it, were it not found in the parallel passages in Matthew and Luke, in neither of whom it is omitted by any MS. or version. See the dissertation on parabolical writing at the end of <reference osisRef="Mat.13.58">Mat 13:58</reference>.
entries.f0a8d19cfc1a612d7fb71d726be53210c18a53fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen39216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39217" type="x-p"/> Know ye not this parable? - The scope and design of which is so very obvious. <div eID="gen39217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39218" type="x-p"/> How then will ye know all parables? - Of which mode of teaching ye should be perfect masters, in order that ye may be able successfully to teach others. This verse is not found in any of the other evangelists.
entries.42a3df70ec4dbcf6229e0fa69ef5fc2b3108f636: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen39218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39219" type="x-p"/> These are they - Probably our Lord here refers to the people to whom he had just now preached, and who, it is likely, did not profit by the word spoken. <div eID="gen39219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39220" type="x-p"/> Where the word is sown - Instead of this clause, four copies of the Itala read the place thus - They who are sown by the way side, are they Who Receive The Word Negligently. There are thousands of this stamp in the Christian world. Reader, art thou one of them?
entries.4b1f04eb42fc985a4e0a66c9a30d5a600ddc6534: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen39220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39221" type="x-p"/> The deceitfulness of riches - This is variously expressed in different copies of the Itala: the errors - delights of the world - completely alienated (abolienati) by the pleasures of the world. The lusts of other things - which have not been included in the anxious cares of the world, and the deceitfulness of riches. All, all, choke the word!
entries.563cedaa7a036a8cab216b800fa817c8d8afc115: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen39221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39222" type="x-p"/> Is a candle - put under a bushel! - The design of my preaching is to enlighten men; my parables not being designed to hide the truth, but to make it more manifest.
entries.1801c129716a30aa66c571e61be4f24732461362: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen39222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39223" type="x-p"/> For there is nothing hid, etc. - Probably our Lord means, that all that had hitherto been secret, relative to the salvation of a lost world, or only obscurely pointed out by types and sacrifices, shall now be uncovered and made plain by the everlasting Gospel. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.5.15">Mat 5:15</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Mat.10.26">Mat 10:26</reference> (note).
entries.f116641d635f2bdd7bfe0c5a41a62a680e5c5561: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen39223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39224" type="x-p"/> And unto you that hear shall more be given - This clause is wanting in DG, Coptic, and four copies of the Itala; and in others, where it is extant, it is variously written. Griesbach has left it out of the text, and supposes it to be a gloss, Whosoever hath, to him shall be given.
entries.a00234a1d2d412bb40af8cfe697ea4a3eaae3055: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen39224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39225" type="x-p"/> He that hath - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.13.12">Mat 13:12</reference> (note).
entries.c882ed89031a4b51f0b6eb6a7bb54c9ca6b9e261: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen39225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39226" type="x-p"/> So is the kingdom of God - This parable is mentioned only by Mark, a proof that Mark did not abridge Matthew. Whitby supposes it to refer to the good ground spoken of before, and paraphrases is thus: - "What I have said of the seed sown upon good ground, may be illustrated by this parable. The doctrine of the kingdom, received in a good and honest heart, is like seed sown by a man in his ground, properly prepared to receive it; for when he hath sown it, he sleeps and wakes day after day, and, looking on it, he sees it spring and grow up through the virtue of the earth in which it is sown, though he knows not how it doth so; and when he finds it ripe, he reaps it, and so receives the benefit of the sown seed. So is it here: the seed sown in the good and honest heart brings forth fruit with patience; and this fruit daily increaseth, though we know not how the Word and Spirit work that increase; and then Christ the husbandman, at the time of the harvest, gathers in this good seed into the kingdom of heaven." I see no necessity of inquiring how Christ may be said to sleep and rise night and day; Christ being like to this husbandman only in sowing and reaping the seed.
entries.80228cde500fe4821b2fadc53d245b035ea363ac: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen39226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39227" type="x-p"/> And should sleep and rise night and day - That is, he should sleep by night, and rise by day; for so the words are obviously to be understood. <div eID="gen39227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39228" type="x-p"/> He knoweth not how - How a plant grows is a mystery in nature, which the wisest philosopher in the universe cannot fully explain.
entries.4b48d611e31d26e22bd54900356ca04048f79a4c: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen39228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39229" type="x-p"/> Bringeth forth - of herself - Αυτοματη. By its own energy, without either the influence or industry of man. Similar to this is the expression of the poet: - <div eID="gen39229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39230" type="x-p"/> Namque aliae, Nullis Homlnum Cogentibus, ipsae <div eID="gen39230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39231" type="x-p"/> Sponte Sua veniunt. <div eID="gen39231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39232" type="x-p"/> Virg. Geor. l. ii. v. 10 "Some (trees) grow of their own accord, without the labor of man." <div eID="gen39232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39233" type="x-p"/> All the endlessly varied herbage of the field is produced in this way. <div eID="gen39233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39234" type="x-p"/> The full corn - Πληρη σιτον, Full wheat; the perfect, full-grown, or ripe corn. Lucian uses κενος καρπος, Empty fruit, for imperfect, or unripe fruit. See Kypke. <div eID="gen39234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39235" type="x-p"/> The kingdom of God, which is generated in the soul by the word of life, under the influence of the Holy Spirit, is first very small; there is only a blade, but this is full of promise, for a good blade shows there is a good seed at bottom, and that the soil in which it is sown is good also. Then the ear - the strong stalk grows up, and the ear is formed at the top; the faith and love of the believing soul increase abundantly; it is justified freely through the redemption that is in Christ; it has the ear which is shortly to be filled with the ripe grain, the outlines of the whole image of God. Then the full corn. The soul is purified from all unrighteousness; and, having escaped the corruption that is in the world, it is made a partaker of the Divine nature, and is filled with all the fullness of God.
entries.f8669599e96511f172bf36528e0a4f710b383559: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen39235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39236" type="x-p"/> He putteth in the sickle - ΑποϚελλει, he sendeth out the sickle, i.e. the reapers; the instrument, by a metonomy, being put for the persons who use it. This is a common figure. It has been supposed that our Lord intimates here that, as soon as a soul is made completely holy, it is taken into the kingdom of God. But certainly the parable does not say so. When the corn is ripe, it is reaped for the benefit of him who sowed it; for it can be of little or no use till it be ripe: so when a soul is saved from all sin, it is capable of being fully employed in the work of the Lord: it is then, and not till then, fully fitted for the Master's use. God saves men to the uttermost, that they may here perfectly love him, and worthily magnify his name. To take them away the moment they are capable of doing this, would be, so far, to deprive the world and the Church of the manifestation of the glory of his grace. "But the text says, he immediately sendeth out the sickle; and this means that the person dies, and is taken into glory, as soon as he is fit for it." No, for there may be millions of cases, where, though to die would be gain, yet to live may be far better for the Church, and for an increase of the life of Christ to the soul. See <reference osisRef="Phi.1.21">Phi 1:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phi.1.24">Phi 1:24</reference>. Besides, if we attempt to make the parable speak here what seems to be implied in the letter, then we may say, with equal propriety, that Christ sleeps and wakes alternately; and that his own grace grows, he knows not how, in the heart in which he has planted it. <div eID="gen39236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39237" type="x-p"/> On these two parables we may remark: - <div eID="gen39237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39238" type="x-p"/> 1. That a preacher is a person employed by God, and sent out to sow the good seed of his kingdom in the souls of men. <div eID="gen39238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39239" type="x-p"/> 2. That it is a sin against God to stay in the field and not sow. <div eID="gen39239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39240" type="x-p"/> 3. That it is a sin to pretend to sow, when a man is not furnished by the keeper of the granary with any more seed. <div eID="gen39240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39241" type="x-p"/> 4. That it is a high offense against God to change the Master's seed, to mix it, or to sow bad seed in the place of it. <div eID="gen39241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39242" type="x-p"/> 5. That he is not a seeds-man of God who desires to sow by the way side, etc., and not on the proper ground, i.e. he who loves to preach only to genteel congregations, to people of sense and fashion, and feels it a pain and a cross to labor among the poor and the ignorant. <div eID="gen39242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39243" type="x-p"/> 6. That he who sows with a simple, upright heart, the seed of his Master, shall (though some may be unfruitful) see the seed take deep root; and, notwithstanding the unfaithfulness and sloth of many of his hearers, he shall doubtless come with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him. See Quesnel.
entries.ae17cb3ec56bba79fdcc63a6157369d2769de09d: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen39243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39244" type="x-p"/> Whereunto shall we liken the kingdom of God? - How amiable is this carefulness of Jesus! How instructive to the preachers of his word! He is not solicitous to seek fine turns of eloquence to charm the minds of his auditors, nor to draw such descriptions and comparisons as may surprise them: but studies only to make himself understood; to instruct to advantage; to give true ideas of faith and holiness; and to find out such expressions as may render necessary truths easy and intelligible to the meanest capacities. The very wisdom of God seems to be at a loss to find out expressions low enough for the slow apprehensions of men. <div eID="gen39244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39245" type="x-p"/> How dull and stupid is the creature! How wise and good the Creator! And how foolish the preacher who uses fine and hard words in his preaching, which, though admired by the shallow, convey no instruction to the multitude.
entries.dc77006b12567501fb83e9fd675b794e1e35892a: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen39245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39246" type="x-p"/> A grain of mustard seed - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.13.31">Mat 13:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.32">Mat 13:32</reference> (note).
entries.298681726a2b101e2a83758f445c0691b1c44ee0: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen39246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39247" type="x-p"/> With many such parables - Πολλαις, many, is omitted by L, sixteen others; the Syriac, both the Persic, one Arabic, Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopic, and two of the Itala. Mill approves of the omission, and Griesbach leaves it doubtful. It is probably an interpolation: the text reads better without it. <div eID="gen39247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39248" type="x-p"/> As they were able to hear - Ακουειν, or to understand always suiting his teaching to the capacities of his hearers. I have always found that preacher most useful, who could adapt his phrase to that of the people to whom he preached. Studying different dialects, and forms of speech, among the common people, is a more difficult and a more useful work than the study of dead languages. The one a man should do, and the other he need not leave undone.
entries.a74e389d115d5b68613b43bbaec70211ec674b93: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen39248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39249" type="x-p"/> He expounded all things to his disciples - That they might be capable of instructing others. Outside hearers, those who do not come into close fellowship with the true disciples of Christ, have seldom more than a superficial knowledge of Divine things. <div eID="gen39249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39250" type="x-p"/> In the fellowship of the saints, where Jesus the teacher is always to be found, every thing is made plain, - for the secret of the Lord is with them who fear him.
entries.daaba7be643780e820dbaac7cd178a08c22e5098: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen39250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39251" type="x-p"/> Let us pass over unto the other side - Our Lord was now by the sea of Galilee.
entries.25543a9c033fc1e280acea2472de257862f48ff8: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen39251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39252" type="x-p"/> They took him even as he was in the ship - That is, the disciples; he was now εν τῳ πλοιῳ, in the boat, i.e. his own boat which usually waited on him, and out of which it appears he was then teaching the people. There were several others there which he might have gone in, had this one not been in the place. The construction of this verse is exceedingly difficult; the meaning appears to be this: - The disciples sailed off with him just as he was in the boat out of which he had been teaching the people; and they did not wait to provide any accommodations for the passage. This I believe to be the meaning of the inspired penman.
entries.5dfe8d5e8c1993523a86e3685593de0c0d7cded2: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen39252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39253" type="x-p"/> A great storm of wind - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.8.24">Mat 8:24</reference> (note).
entries.2bf0f87fef49b456d34e4e28d5a6dd8d6a4b7484: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen39253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39254" type="x-p"/> On a pillow - Προσκεφαλαιον probably means a little bed, or hammock, such as are common in small vessels. I have seen several in small packets, or passage boats, not a great deal larger than a bolster.
entries.647a82c98a9e071eeefb225d0aedb68714dce5eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen39254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39255" type="x-p"/> Peace, be still - Be silent! Be still! There is uncommon majesty and authority in these words. Who but God could act thus? Perhaps this salvation of his disciples in the boat might be designed to show forth that protection and deliverance which Christ will give to his followers, however violently they may be persecuted by earth or hell. At least, this is a legitimate use which may be made of this transaction.
entries.55620ce62b78bb3bcb21f86e37d982ddfcc3dc8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen39255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39256" type="x-p"/> Why are ye so fearful? - Having me with you. <div eID="gen39256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39257" type="x-p"/> How is it that ye have no faith? - Having already had such proofs of my unlimited power and goodness.
entries.7688551de7b5f273e60b683077f0bcea540f7468: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen39257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39258" type="x-p"/> What manner of man is this? - They were astonished at such power proceeding from a person who appeared to be only like one of themselves. It is often profitable to entertain each other with the succor and support which we receive from God in times of temptation and distress; and to adore, with respectful awe, that sovereign power and goodness by which we have been delivered. <div eID="gen39258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39259" type="x-p"/> Having spoken so largely of the spiritual and practical uses to be made of these transactions, where the parallel places occur in the preceding evangelist, I do not think it necessary to repeat those things here.  <chapter eID="Mark.4"/> <div eID="gen39259" type="x-p"/>

Verse 25. For he that hath, Mt 13:12. The meaning here seems to be--He that diligently attends to my words, shall increase more and more in the knowledge of the truth; but he that neglects them, and is inattentive, shall become more ignorant; the few things which he had learned he will forget, and his trifling knowledge will be diminished.

It is not sufficient that we have learned some things, or appear to have learned much. entries.377262c2406839869984a9a6c4bc4d6dee363f38:
Verse 27. And should sleep, and rise night and day. Should sleep in the night, and rise by day, for so the expression is to be understood. That is, should live in his usual way, without exerting any influence over the growing grain. By this we are not to infer that men are to use no diligence in the obtainment and growth of piety; but the illustration shows this, and this only, that as we cannot tell how grain grows, so we cannot tell the mode in which piety increases in the heart.

He knoweth not how. This is still true. After all the researches of philosophers, not one has been able to tell the way in which grain grows. They can observe one fact after another; they can see the changes; they can see the necessity of rains and suns, of care and shelter, but beyond this they cannot go. So in religion. We can mark the change; we can see the need of prayer, and examination, and searching the Scriptures, and the ordinances of religion, but we cannot tell in what way the religious principle is strengthened. As God unseen, yet by the use of proper means, makes the grass to flourish, so God unseen, but by proper means, nourishes the soul, and the plants of piety spring up, and bloom, and bear fruit. See Jn 3:8.
entries.cfe804b95b45ddb2113bfbcc3474c9daaa93e5ec:
Verse 28. For the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself. That is, it is done without the power of man. It is done while man is engaged in other things. The scope of the place does not require us to suppose that our Saviour meant to say that the earth had any productive power of itself, but only that it produced its fruits not by the power of man. God gives it its power. It has no power of its own. So religion in the heart is not by the power of man. It grows he cannot tell how; and of course he cannot, without Divine aid, control it. It is by the power of God. At the same time, as without industry man would have no harvest, so without active effort he would have no religion. Both are connected with his effort; both are to be measured commonly by his effort, (Php 2:12) both grow he cannot tell how; both increase when the proper means are used; and both depend on God for increase.

First the blade. The green, tender shoot, that first starts out of the earth, before the stalk is formed.

Then the ear. The original means, the stalk or spire of wheat or barley, as well as the ear.

The full corn. The ripe wheat. The grain swollen to its proper size. By this is denoted, undoubtedly, that grace or religion in the heart is of gradual growth. It is at first tender, feeble, perhaps almost imperceptible, like the first shootings of the grain in the earth. Perhaps also, like grain, it often lies long in the earth before there are signs of life. Like the tender grain, also, it needs care, kindness, and culture. A light frost, a cold storm, or a burning sun, alike injure it. So tender piety, in the heart of a child, needs care, kindness, culture. It needs shelter from the frosts and storms of a cold, unfeeling world. It needs the genial dews and mild suns of heaven. In other words, it needs instruction, prayer, and friendly counsel from parents, teachers, ministers, and experienced Christians, that it may grow, and bring forth the full fruits of holiness. Like the grain also, in due time, it will grow strong; it will produce its appropriate fruit--a full and rich harvest, to the praise of God.

entries.e91431ec89e421a64c5e67ab60173900c487fa46:
Verse 29. Immediately he putteth in the sickle. This is the way with the husbandman. As soon as the grain is ripe, it is cut down. So it is often with the Christian. As soon as he is prepared for heaven, he is taken there. But we are not to press this part of the parable, as if it meant that all are removed as soon as they are fit for heaven. Every parable contains circumstances thrown in to fill up the story, which cannot be literally interpreted. In this, the circumstance of sleeping and rising cannot be applied to Christ; and in like manner the harvest, I suppose, is not to be literally interpreted. Perhaps the whole parable may be differently interpreted. The seed sown may mean the gospel which he was preaching. In Judea its beginnings were small. Yet he would leave it; commit it to his disciples; and return to his Father. The gospel in the meantime, left by him, would take root, spring up, and produce an abundant harvest. In due time he would return, send forth the angels, and gather in the harvest, and save his people for ever.

entries.191e042af2a749000797ac9498609da9104bf75c:
Verse 30. Whereunto shall we liken, etc. This shows the great solicitude which Jesus had to adapt his instructions to the capacity of his disciples, he sought out the most plain and striking illustrations-- an example which should be followed by all the ministers of the gospel. At the same time that the instructions of the pulpit should be dignified--as our Saviour's always were--they should be plain, adapted to the capacity of the audience, and easily understood. To do this, the following things are necessary in a minister:

(1.) Humility. A freedom from a desire to shine, and astonish the world by the splendour of his talents, and by his learning and eloquence.

(2.) Good sense. A satisfaction in being understood.

(3.) Acquaintance with the habits of thought and manner of speaking among the people. To do this, frequent intercourse with them is necessary.

(4.) A good, sound education. It is the men of ignorance, with some smattering of learning, and with a desire to confound and astonish men by the use of unintelligible words, and by the introduction of matter that is wholly unconnected with the subject, that most often shoot over the heads of the people. Preachers of humility; good sense, and education, are content with being understood, and free from the affectation of saying things to amaze and confound their auditors.

entries.76f50294b3a14a53aa6d876cb1b22cfe6829dde6: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.4.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.4.12" sID="gen99156" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99157" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.4.12">Mark 4:12</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">That seeing, they may see, and not perceive.</hi> Here it may suffice to state briefly what has already been fully explained, that the doctrine is not, strictly speaking, or by itself, or in its own nature, but by accident, the cause of blindness. When persons of a weak sight come out into sunshine, their eyes become dimmer than before, and that defect is in no way attributed to the sun, but to their eyes. In like manner, when the word of God blinds and hardens the reprobate, as this takes place through their own depravity, it belongs truly and naturally to themselves, but is accidental, as respects the word.<div eID="gen99157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99158" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Lest at any time they should be converted.</hi> This clause points out the advantage that is gained by <hi type="italic">seeing and understanding</hi> It is, that men, having been <hi type="italic">converted </hi>to God, are restored to his favor, and, being reconciled to him, enjoy prosperity and happiness. The true end for which<div eID="gen99158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen99159" type="x-p"/>God desires that his word should be preached is, to reconcile men to himself by renewing their minds and hearts. With respect to the reprobate, on the other hand, Isaiah here declares that the stony hardness remains in them, so that they do not obtain mercy, and that the word fails to produce its effect upon them, so as to soften their minds to repentance.<div eID="gen99159" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.4.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99156" osisID="Mark.4.12" type="section"/>
entries.a3a5533b25556845bfe37096ca0e4c84f6d0a222: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.4.26" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.4.26" sID="gen99286" type="section"/> <div sID="gen99287" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.4.26">Mark 4:26</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">So is the kingdom of God.</hi> Though this comparison has the same object with the two immediately preceding, yet Christ appears to direct his discourse purposely to the ministers of the word, that they may not grow indifferent about the discharge of their duty, because the fruit of their labor does not immediately appear. He holds out for their imitation the example of husbandmen, who <hi type="italic">throw seed into the ground</hi> with the expectation of reaping, and do not torment themselves with uneasiness and anxiety, but go to bed and rise again; or, in other words, pursue their ordinary and daily toil, till the corn arrive at maturity in due season. In like manner, though the seed of the word be concealed and choked for a time, Christ enjoins pious teachers to be of good courage, and not to allow their alacrity to be slackened through distrust.<div eID="gen99287" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.4.26" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen99286" osisID="Mark.4.26" type="section"/>

Some bring forth the Fruit of Faith and Holiness, and the abiding Fruit of it, tho in different Degrees. But many, yea the most of those that hear it, either bring fo<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>th no Fruit, or no abiding Fruit, (which is indeed no true Fruit.) The Causes of this are, some Mens perfunctory, and c<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>reless hearing, never regarding to meditate on it, apply it to their own So<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ls, or to hide it in their Memories. Others not suffering it to Sink into their Hearts, and to take Root in them, tho it may at present a little affect them, and make them matter of Discourse. Other Mens thoughts being taken up with business, and the care of this world, and their hearts filled with the love of the things of this Life, which they cannot part with when trouble and persecution for the owning, and Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fession of the Gospel ariseth. 3. It likewise teacheth us a sure note of unprofitable hearers of the Word, as also of those, whom the Word is likely to profit, and have any good, and saving effect upon, the former hear, but never regard whether they understand what they hear, yea or no. The others are not satisfied with hear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, unless they understand, for those who went to him to know the <ns0:hi>Parable,</ns0:hi> were not the <ns0:hi>twelve only,</ns0:hi> (who are often called his Disciples emphatically) but those others that were about him, to whom <ns0:hi>it was given to know the Mysteries of the Kingdom of God.</ns0:hi> 4.                   <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:280" />21 And he said unto them, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 8.16. <ns0:hi>A Measure <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">

                        </ns0:gap>ntaining sixteen sexta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />

                        </ns0:gap>. viz.</ns0:hi> M<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>tth. 5.15.</ns0:note> Is a candel brought to be put under a bushel, or under a bed? and not to be set on a candlestick?<ns0:note place="bottom">The import of this verse may be learned from <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.15, 16. where the words are, and applyed by an <ns0:hi>Exhortation</ns0:hi> to holiness, being an Argument drawn from the <ns0:hi>End,</ns0:hi> for which Men receive Gifts and Grace from God, which is not only for their own advan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tage, tho (like the Husbandman) those that have it, reap first of their own fruit, but for the good, and advantage of others also. Some think that Christ here speaketh of himself, who is the <ns0:hi>Light of the World,</ns0:hi> and therefore opened this Parable unto them. But the context in <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> guiding us to the true sense of the Words, I see no reason for us to busy our selves in searching out another, especially when the connexion is so fair with the foregoing Words, where he had been describing the good ground by bringing forth fruit, some <ns0:hi>thirty,</ns0:hi> some <ns0:hi>sixty,</ns0:hi> some an <ns0:hi>hundred fold.</ns0:hi> What there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore the sowing the seed in the good ground, mentioned in the Parable is, that is the lighting up of a Candel in this verse, and the Light shewed by the lighted Candel, not put under a Vessel, or a Bed, but in a Candlestick, is the same thing with the Fruit before mentioned.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 8.17.</ns0:note> For there is nothing hid which shall not be manifested, neither was any thing kept secret, but that it should come abroad.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 11.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> If any man have ears to hear let him hear.<ns0:note place="bottom">Our Saviour <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 10.26. sending out his <ns0:hi>Apostles,</ns0:hi> saith to them. <ns0:hi>Fear them not therefore,</ns0:hi> that is, not your Enemies, and Persecutors, <ns0:hi>for there is nothing covered, that shall not be reveal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, and hid, that shall not be known,</ns0:hi> the sense of which Words, we there said might be, tho your innocency be now hid, yet it shall be made known, or tho the Gospel be now hid, and Preached in a little corner, and kept secret, it shall be made manifest, and come abroad. Both <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke,</ns0:hi> have it immediately after the Parable of the Sower, where it doth not seem to have the same sense as here. But more general Proverbial common sayings, may be variously applyed to things, to which the common sense, and import of them will agree. Some here apply them thus. There is nothing in the Prophesies concerning me, which shall not be ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifested, which agrees with the sense of those who interpret the former verse concerning Christ, as if he had been giving a reason, why he opened the Parables to those that asked him of it. But those who interpret it to the sense which it beareth plainly, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.15.16. make the sense thus, for tho you may play the Hypo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />crites, and under a profession of the Gospel, but hide the Hypo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />crisie, Lusts and Corruptions of your Hearts, yet that Mask will not hold always, there will come a day of Judgment, which will mani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fest and discover all; and bring to light the <ns0:hi>hidden things of dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />honesty,</ns0:hi> what we have <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 23. is but an usual conclusion which our Saviour hath often made of any grave, and important dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />courses.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 And he said unto them, Take heed what you <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 8.18.</ns0:note> hear, With what measure you mete, it shall be mea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sured to you, and unto you that hear shall more be given.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 For he that hath, to him shall be given, and he that hath not, from him shall be taken, even that which he hath.<ns0:note place="bottom">Whoso considereth the connexion of these Words. <ns0:hi>With what measure you Mete,</ns0:hi> &c. With the first Words in the verse. <ns0:hi>Take heed what you hear,</ns0:hi> and compares the former with the Paralel Texts, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 7.2. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 6.38. will wonder what the force should be of the Argument. For in both the Paralell Texts, the latter Words in this verse seem to be used as an Argument to per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swade them to <ns0:hi>Iustice,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Charity</ns0:hi> towards Men, from the Pu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nishments of the Violations of the Law concerning them, by way of <ns0:hi>Retaliatio<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> Nor are there any Sins so ordinarily as those of that kind, so Punished. But they can have no such force here, following those words, <ns0:hi>Take heed what you hear.</ns0:hi> But as I said before, there is nothing more usual then divers applications of the same common saying, or <ns0:hi>Proverbial expression,</ns0:hi> the saying is true, whether it be understood of Men, or of God. <ns0:hi>As we deal with God, so will God deal with us. Take heed what you hear, Luke</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>how you hear. Take heed what you hear,</ns0:hi> as much as take heed to what you hear, that you may <ns0:hi>receive</ns0:hi> the Word not as Seed by the Way side, or in Thorny, or Stony ground, but as in good ground. This seemeth rather to be the sense of our Saviour, then to give a caution by these Words, to Men to examine what they hear, searching the Scriptures, whether what they hear doth agree with them, tho that also be the Duty of all Conscientious Persons, as appeareth from <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 17.11. For saith our Saviour, God will deal with you as to his Providence, as you deal with him. If you allow the Word of God but a <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ghtly hearing, you shall reap from it heard, a very slightly profit, and advantage, this appeareth to be the sense, from the following Words. <ns0:hi>And unto you that hear shall more be given,</ns0:hi> that is, unto you that <ns0:hi>hear,</ns0:hi> so as you <ns0:hi>attend, understand, believe, hearken,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>obey.</ns0:hi> God will give further knowledge of Divine Mysteries. <ns0:hi>For he that hath, to him shall be given,</ns0:hi> &c. Another general Proverbial expre<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>sion, which the Reader may find opened in the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 13.12 <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 25.29.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 And he said, So is the Kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the ground.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 And should sleep, and rise night and day, and the seed should spring, and grow up he knoweth not how.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 For the earth bringeth forth fruit of her self, first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 But when the fruit is <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Ripe.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> brought forth, immediate<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly he putteth in the sickle because the harvest is come.<ns0:note place="bottom">Our Evangelist alone taketh notice of this Parable, nor hath it any particular explication annexed, if we expound it with relation to what went before, the Scope of it seemeth to be, to let us know that God will have an account of Men for their hearing of his Word, and therefore Men had need to take heed <ns0:hi>what they hear,</ns0:hi> (as <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith) and how they hear (as <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> phraseth it) thus the 29 verse expoundeth the former with the help of our S<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>viours exposition of the <ns0:hi>Parable</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Tares,</ns0:hi> on which he had told us, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 13.39. <ns0:hi>The harvest is the end of the World. The reapers are the Angels.</ns0:hi> There is another notion of Gods harvest, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 9.37. and <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 4.35. where <ns0:hi>Gods harvest</ns0:hi> signifies a People in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clined, and prepared to hear, and to receive the Gospel. But withal this <ns0:hi>Parable</ns0:hi> of our Saviours may be of further use to us. <ns0:hi>The Kingdom of God is,</ns0:hi> &c. That is, such is the Providential dispensation of God, in gathering his Church by the Ministry of the Word, as mens casting of seed into the ground; when the Husbandman hath cast his seed into the ground, he is no more sollicitous about it, nor doth he expect to discern the motion of it, but having done what is his part, he <ns0:hi>sleepeth,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>riseth again,</ns0:hi> leaving the issue to Gods Providence, the <ns0:hi>Earth brings forth Fruit of it self,</ns0:hi> yet not without the influence of Heaven, both in the shining of the Sun, and the falling of the Dew, and of the Rain, neither doth its fruit appear presently in its full ripeness and per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fection, but gradually is made perfect; first there appears the <ns0:hi>Blade,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Herb,</ns0:hi> then the <ns0:hi>Ear,</ns0:hi> then the <ns0:hi>Grain,</ns0:hi> which by degrees groweth to its full Magnitude, and then hardeneth, and then the Husbandman putteth in his Sickle; so the Ministers of the Gospel ought faithfully to do their Parts, in sowing the seed of the Gospel, then not to be too sollicitous, but to leave the issue unto God; where the seed falls upon <ns0:hi>good Ground,</ns0:hi> the Word will not be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fruitful, the Minister of the Gospel doth not presently discern the fruit of his labour, he at first, it may be, seeth nothing of it, but is ready to cry out, <ns0:hi>I have laboured in vain,</ns0:hi> but tho the seed lie under the clods, and seems choaked with the corruption of Mans heart, yet if the <ns0:hi>Soul</ns0:hi> be one to whom it is given <ns0:hi>to know the Mysteries of the Kingdom of God,</ns0:hi> it shall Spring out, the Word will be found not to be lost; but first will <ns0:hi>Spring</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Blade,</ns0:hi> then will <ns0:hi>appear the Ear</ns0:hi>; the Fruit of the Word Preached appears by degrees, sometimes at first only by creating good inclinations in the Souls, and desires to learn the way of the Lord more perfectly, then in acts further tending to perfection, at last in confirmed habits of Grace. It is not thus with all, in some the Word brings forth nothing, but the <ns0:hi>Blade,</ns0:hi> a little outward Profession, which dwindleth away and dyes, in some the Profession holds longer, but they never come to confirmed habits of Virtue and holiness. But there will come an Harvest when God will come with his Sickle, to reap the Fruit of his Seed Sown; therefore Men had need take heed <ns0:hi>what</ns0:hi> and how <ns0:hi>they hear.</ns0:hi> This I take to be the sense of this <ns0:hi>Parable.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>

               <ns0:p n="34">34 But without a parable, Spake he not unto them, and when they were alone, he expounded all things to his disciples.<ns0:note place="bottom">From hence we may gather that all the <ns0:hi>Parables</ns0:hi> by which on Saviour instructed his hearers are not recorded by the Evangelists tho many bee, and some mentioned by one, some by two of them, which are not recorded by the other, <ns0:hi>as they were able to hear it.</ns0:hi> Christ disdained not to accommodate his stile, and method of Preaching<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> to his hearers capacity, neither will any faithful Minister or Christ do it, he Preacheth in the best stile, Language and Me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thod that Preacheth best to the capacity, understanding and profit of his hearers. Other Preachers do indeed but trif<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>le with the greate<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
